title: Becoming a disk jockey on KHON and the sextet's tenor player
summary: He was trained by Larry Grant as a DJ on a Honolulu AM station and sneaked jazz in, and names Pete Peterson on tenor.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Also, it was during this period that Larry Grant, who used to do the remotes from Lai Yi Chai's, where we played, decided I had a nice sound for radio, so he took me under his wing and trained me to be a disk jockey. So for a while I was a disk jockey on KHON, which was the local equivalent of KKGO, only it was an AM station, and...

Not all Jazz. It was all kinds of music. So I could play...well, anything that came to mind. Naturally I'd sneak in a little Jazz now and then. But the thing that people don't understand about Honolulu and Jazz is that people don't go to Honolulu to hear Jazz. They go to hear Hawaiian guitars and local music. So Jazz has a rough time there, like anywhere else. I suppose what I played, I guess I'd call it Jazz, but mostly it was Pop tunes just arranged in the way I felt...in my own way. So you can be sneaky and play Jazz anyhow!
How long were you a disk jockey?
Oh, I guess about seven-eight months.
Again, that's something I didn't know.
Another surprise. But it was fun. I learned how, you know, work the board, and I didn't knock the station off the air too much -- I finally got it figured out. But that was fun.

Let's see, who else did I miss? Pete Peterson was the tenor saxophone player. He was...his roots were Chinese and Hawaiian. My alto player was full Chinese. Why can't I think of his name? I'll come back to that later.
Let's see, who else was in the band... Yeah, and me. I played the bass. I didn't have my tuba at that time, so I just played the bass and wrote music every day.
